name: Sulfacetamide
lead: Sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic used on the eyes and skin. [1][2] In dermatology it is most often sold as sodium sulfacetamide, frequently combined with sulfur, for acne vulgaris, rosacea with papules and pustules, and seborrheic dermatitis. [3][2]

A review of topical acne agents and the US product label describe it as a prescription topical option; reported hypersensitivity is uncommon, but the label carries warnings about Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people. [3][4] No clinical trials of it are summarised in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Klaron, Ovace, Plexion, Clenia, Avar, Bleph-10 [2]

paras: The US label for sodium sulfacetamide with sulfur indicates it for topical control of acne vulgaris, acne rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis. [4] Wikipedia notes the sulfur combination is commonly promoted for rosacea with papules or pustules, with sulfur acting as a keratolytic. [2] Common product concentrations are 10% sulfacetamide, often with 5% sulfur, as lotions, washes or cleansers. [1]
It is also used in eye drops and ointments for bacterial conjunctivitis. [1][2]

The most common effects are local stinging, burning, irritation, dryness and peeling. [2][1] The label says irritation and hypersensitivity reports are uncommon, but notes Stevens-Johnson syndrome has occurred with sulfonamides including topical sodium sulfacetamide, and that drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus from topical use has been reported, in one case fatal. [4] Products are not for people sensitive to sulfur or sulfa drugs. [2]
Sulfacetamide competes with para-aminobenzoic acid and inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, blocking bacterial folic acid synthesis and slowing growth (bacteriostatic). [2][1]

card.summary: An old sulfa antibiotic, usually paired with sulfur in prescription lotions and washes for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.
card.note: Not for people allergic to sulfa drugs; rare serious skin reactions are on the label.

quick.overview:
Sodium sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic applied to the skin, often combined with sulfur, for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.

It is a prescription product in the US, and the sources reviewed describe its role rather than citing trial results.
quick.mechanism: It blocks bacterial folic acid synthesis to slow bacterial growth; sulfur adds a keratolytic effect.
quick.risks: Mild stinging, dryness and irritation are most common. The US label warns of Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people and reports of drug-induced lupus, including one fatal case.
